title: paged KV cache: block manager improvements (allocator, reuse, pinning)
author: Asha Patel
release_notes: Improves paged KV cache block allocator for lower p99 latency and reduced memory churn; adds pinning API for hot KV prefixes and safety guardrails for gradual rollout.
description:
Context and motivation: The paged KV cache has been a major lever for reducing token-level cost by reusing KV cache across requests, but we observed two recurring issues in production: 1) allocator fragmentation and frequent small allocations caused CPU overhead and memory churn during sustained traffic, increasing p99 latency; 2) hot prefixes were getting evicted under bursty workloads, causing repeated recomputation and increased tail latency. This change implements a set of block manager improvements to address fragmentation, support efficient reuse, and expose a safe pinning primitive for hot entries.

Summary of changes: - Introduces a paged block allocator with free-list buckets and a lightweight bitmap index for O(1) allocation of fixed-size blocks. - Adds a fast path for block reuse by tracking recently freed blocks per shard and amortizing decommit work. - Implements a pinning API that allows callers to mark KV pages as pinned, preventing eviction for a configurable lease duration. Pins are tracked with a versioned pin-count to avoid ABA issues. - Improves eviction heuristics: combines recency + dynamic hotness score computed from access counters sampled per-request. - Adds a conservative slow-path for large contiguous KV slices that fall outside fixed block sizes (spill-to-heap with background compaction). - Adds unit, integration and microbenchmark coverage and a rollout flag to enable the new manager gradually.

Design details: - Block allocator: We moved from variable sized chunk allocations to a power-of-two block allocator layered on top of the existing paged storage. Blocks are 4KB/16KB/64KB buckets chosen by request size. Each shard maintains per-bucket freelists and a 64-bit bitmap index for quick existence checks. Allocation acquires a shard-local spinlock; hot-path allocations avoid heap allocations and use preallocated slab pages. This reduces syscalls and contention for typical request sizes.

- Reuse strategy: Deallocations append to a hot per-shard ring buffer of recently freed blocks. The allocator first consumes from the ring buffer before touching global freelists, which avoids cross-thread contention when multiple inference workers release blocks concurrently. We also added a deferred reclamation window to avoid immediate reuse of still-referenced pages by background tasks.

- Pinning API: Pinning is cooperative. Callers can request a pin on a KV prefix with lease_ms and an optional priority. Pinned pages increment a versioned counter stored alongside block metadata. Eviction logic honors pin counts and will only evict pinned pages when forced via explicit admin override. When a pin expires we decrement the counter asynchronously to avoid blocking fast paths. The pin API exposes metrics for pin_count and pin_evictions to help operators tune lease durations.

- Eviction & heuristics: Eviction now scores pages by a combination of recency and sampled access frequency over a sliding window. Pages below a dynamic score threshold become eligible for eviction. The threshold adapts based on free memory pressure. Hot pages identified by high score are automatically offered for pin candidate recommendations in observability.

- Safety & rollout: Changes are behind a feature flag kv_block_manager_v2 with three modes: off, staged, and forced. In staged mode the new allocator runs for a subset of shards (configurable), and metrics are emitted to compare allocations, fragmentation, and tail latency. We include runtime checks that fallback to legacy manager on repeated allocation errors.

Commits summary: - commit 1: core: add paged block allocator and bucketed freelists (major codepath) - commit 2: core: per-shard ring buffer for fast reuse and deferred reclamation - commit 3: api: pinning primitives and metrics + admin endpoints - commit 4: eviction: adaptive score-based eviction and integration tests - commit 5: benchmarks: microbench harness and perf test cases + docs - commit 6: tests: unit and integration tests; CI fixes and flake addresses

Files changed (high-level): - inference/kv_cache/block_manager.* (allocator, metadata, pin tracking) - inference/kv_cache/eviction_policy.* (scoring, adaptive thresholds) - inference/kv_cache/pinning_api.* (public API surface and HTTP admin) - runtime/shard_manager.* (shard-local freelist integration) - metrics/kv_cache.metrics (pins, evictions, allocation_latency) - bench/kv_cache_microbench (bench harness and runner) - tests/kv_cache/* (unit and integration tests) - docs/runtimes/kv_cache.md (design and rollout guide)

Small illustrative diff snippets (kept short): - block_manager.cpp: added allocate_block(bucket) fast-path using bitmap test_and_set - pinning_api.go: New RPC PinPrefix(prefix, lease_ms) -> {pin_id} - eviction_policy.cc: compute_score(page) now samples accesses with exponential decay

Tests and benchmarks: - Unit tests for allocator buckets, concurrency correctness, pin refcounts, and eviction thresholds. - Integration test scenario that replays real request traces to validate reuse and pin behaviour under burst. - Microbenchmarks show p50 generation latency unchanged, p99 improved by ~18% on our 256-client stress harness with content reuse, and metadata CPU cycles reduced by ~22%. Memory fragmentation reduced by 28% in the synthetic fragmentation test. Detailed numbers are attached to the benchmark artifact in CI.

Backward compatibility and migration: - The on-disk/serialized KV page format is compatible; we maintained the page header versioning. - Ops can toggle kv_block_manager_v2 per-cluster; we recommend staged rollout for high-volume customers. - Pinning is additive and requires explicit usage from higher-level schedulers; we do not pin automatically without operator opt-in.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed and linked - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Integration tests added - [x] Benchmarks added - [x] Metrics and dashboards updated - [x] Feature flag and staged rollout path implemented - [x] Observability: pin metrics and eviction events emitted

Review conversation (abridged): - James Lowe: Please include metrics for allocation latencies and fragmentation over time. Also call out worst-case lock hold time on allocation path. Author reply: Added histograms allocation_latency_ms and freelist_lock_hold_ns, updated benchmarks section. - Priya Raman: Concern about pin leaks causing memory retention. Requested automatic recovery path when pin counts remain after lease expiry for more than 5x lease. Author reply: Implemented asynchronous pin expiry cleanup and admin 'force-unpin' endpoint with audit log. Added tests simulating leaked pins. - Liam O'Connor: Questioned the complexity of ring buffer and whether it adds more failure modes. Author reply: Verified correctness with stress tests and added deferred reclamation to avoid ABA and reuse races. - Priya Raman: Approved after pin leak mitigation and added metrics. - James Lowe: Approved after CI passed and perf numbers verified on perf-canary.

CI summary: - linux-unit-tests: pass - linux-integration-tests: pass (integration env replay used sample traces) - perf-canary: pass with improved p99 numbers in canary region - linters: pass after two minor fixes - flakefix: one transient test rerun required, fixed in commit 6

Merge outcome: Merged to main via squash. PR accompanies a short design doc and an observability dashboard dashboard link in release notes. Rollout plan: enable staged mode for perf-canary, monitor allocation_latency_ms, kv_fragmentation_ratio, p99_generation_latency. If regressions seen, revert with feature flag off.

Notes for future work: - Explore per-request predictive pinning from the scheduler based on upcoming prefixes. - Investigate opportunistic compaction during low utilization windows to reclaim large contiguous spans. - Consider exporting detailed allocation traces for more fine-grained postmortem analysis.
